title: Reconstructing a Community Irrigation Network
transcript:
When historians study a rural irrigation network, they are studying more than a set of physical channels. They are also examining agreements about access, maintenance, and responsibility. Today I want to show how different kinds of evidence can be combined to reconstruct such a system without giving one source more certainty than it deserves.

The investigation might begin with maps made at different dates. These can reveal when a branch of the network first appeared in official records. However, a feature missing from a map was not necessarily absent on the ground. The mapmaker may have omitted small structures or focused only on property boundaries.

Fieldwork provides another kind of evidence. Researchers can follow surviving channels and record changes in their width, depth, or construction. A narrow section lined with newer material might indicate a repair, but it could also reflect a change in use. The physical trace needs to be interpreted alongside other information.

Local committee minutes may explain who was expected to maintain particular sections. They sometimes record disagreements more clearly than ordinary routines, because a dispute required a formal decision. This creates an important bias: a period with many surviving complaints may have been well documented rather than unusually uncooperative.

To investigate how water was shared, historians could compare meeting records with household accounts and crop records. A rule assigning equal hours of access would not necessarily give every field the same amount of water. Distance, leakage, and the timing of delivery could all affect what actually reached a farm.

Interviews with residents may help identify local names that do not appear on official plans. A place described in an old record as the upper gate might be known by a different name today. Interview evidence can connect those references, although memories of events before a person's lifetime must be distinguished from direct experience.

The final reconstruction should show both what is known and what remains uncertain. On a digital map, for example, confirmed channel routes could be displayed differently from proposed connections. Drawing every line with equal confidence would make the result look tidy while hiding the quality of the underlying evidence.

Such a study can also inform current discussions about shared resources. It may reveal practical ways communities organised maintenance, but it should not turn the past into an ideal model. People with less land or less influence may have had limited opportunities to leave records. Recognising that absence is essential when assessing whose interests the network actually served.

questions.prompt: Why might many recorded complaints be misleading?
options: They may reflect detailed documentation rather than more conflict
They prove that the network never worked
They always refer to unrelated villages
questions.answer: They may reflect detailed documentation rather than more conflict
questions.explanation: 投诉数量多可能只是记录充分，不一定冲突更多。

questions.prompt: How should uncertainty be shown in the final map?
options: By distinguishing confirmed and proposed routes
questions.answer: By distinguishing confirmed and proposed routes
questions.explanation: 应使用不同显示方式区分确定路线和推测连接。
